verses.zh: 保罗和西拉经过暗妃坡里、亚波罗尼亚，来到帖撒罗尼迦，在那里有犹太人的会堂。
verses.en: After they traveled through[NOTE:1] Amphipolis[NOTE:2] and Apollonia,[NOTE:3] they came to Thessalonica,[NOTE:4] where there was a Jewish synagogue.[NOTE:5]
notes: BDAG 250 s.v. διοδεύω 1 has “go, travel through” for this verse.
Amphipolis. The capital city of the southeastern district of Macedonia (BDAG 55 s.v. ᾿Αμφίπολις). It was a military post. From Philippi this was about 33 mi (53 km).
Apollonia was a city in Macedonia about 27 mi (43 km) west southwest of Amphipolis.

Thessalonica (modern Salonica) was a city in Macedonia about 33 mi (53 km) west of Apollonia. It was the capital of Macedonia. The road they traveled over was called the Via Egnatia. It is likely they rode horses, given their condition in Philippi. The implication of v. 1 is that the two previously mentioned cities lacked a synagogue.map For location see JP1-C1; JP2-C1; JP3-C1; JP4-C1.
See the note on synagogue in 6:9.

verses.zh: 保罗照他素常的规矩进去，一连三个安息日，本着圣经与他们辩论，
verses.en: Paul went to the Jews in the synagogue,[NOTE:1] as he customarily did, and on three Sabbath days he addressed[NOTE:2] them from the scriptures,
notes: Grk “he went in to them”; the referent (the Jews in the synagogue) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Although the word διελέξατο (dielexato; from διαλέγομαι, dialegomai) is frequently translated “reasoned,” “disputed,” or “argued,” this sense comes from its classical meaning where it was used of philosophical disputation, including the Socratic method of questions and answers. However, there does not seem to be contextual evidence for this kind of debate in Acts 17:2. As G. Schrenk (TDNT 2:94-95) points out, “What is at issue is the address which any qualified member of a synagogue might give.” Other examples of this may be found in the NT in Matt 4:23 and Mark 1:21.

verses.zh: 讲解陈明基督必须受害，从死里复活；又说：「我所传与你们的这位耶稣就是基督。」
verses.en: explaining and demonstrating[NOTE:1] that the Christ[NOTE:2] had to suffer and to rise from the dead,[NOTE:3] saying,[NOTE:4] “This Jesus I am proclaiming to you is the Christ.”[NOTE:5]
notes: BDAG 772 s.v. παρατίθημι 2.b has “demonstrate, point out” here.
Or “Messiah”; both “Christ” (Greek) and “Messiah” (Hebrew and Aramaic) mean “one who has been anointed.”sn See the note on Christ in 2:31.

The Christ had to suffer and to rise from the dead. These two points (suffering and resurrection) would have been among the more controversial aspects of Paul’s messianic preaching. The term translated “had to” (δεῖ, dei) shows how divine design and scripture corresponded here.

The Greek words used here (καὶ ὅτι, kai hoti, “and that”) mark the switch from indirect to direct discourse. Contemporary English requires the use of an introductory verb of speaking or saying to make this transition.

Or “Messiah”; both “Christ” (Greek) and “Messiah” (Hebrew and Aramaic) mean “one who has been anointed.”sn See the note on Christ in 2:31. The identification of the Messiah with Jesus indicates Paul was proclaiming the fulfillment of messianic promise.

verses.zh: 他们中间有些人听了劝，就附从保罗和西拉，并有许多虔敬的希腊人，尊贵的妇女也不少。
verses.en: Some of them were persuaded[NOTE:1] and joined Paul and Silas, along with a large group[NOTE:2] of God-fearing Greeks[NOTE:3] and quite a few[NOTE:4] prominent women.
notes: Or “convinced.”
Or “a large crowd.”

Or “of devout Greeks,” but this is practically a technical term for the category called God-fearers, Gentiles who worshiped the God of Israel and in many cases kept the Mosaic law, but did not take the final step of circumcision necessary to become a proselyte to Judaism. See further K. G. Kuhn, TDNT 6:732-34, 743-44. Luke frequently mentions such people (Acts 13:43, 50; 16:14; 17:17; 18:7).
Grk “not a few”; this use of negation could be misleading to the modern English reader, however, and so has been translated as “quite a few” (which is the actual meaning of the expression).

verses.zh: 但那不信的犹太人心里嫉妒，招聚了些市井匪类，搭伙成群，耸动合城的人闯进耶孙的家，要将保罗、西拉带到百姓那里。
verses.en: But the Jews became jealous,[NOTE:1] and gathering together some worthless men from the rabble in the marketplace,[NOTE:2] they formed a mob[NOTE:3] and set the city in an uproar.[NOTE:4] They attacked Jason’s house,[NOTE:5] trying to find Paul and Silas[NOTE:6] to bring them out to the assembly.[NOTE:7]
notes: Grk “becoming jealous.” The participle ζηλώσαντες (zēlōsantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. So elsewhere in Acts (5:17; 7:9; 13:45).

Literally ἀγοραῖος (agoraios) refers to the crowd in the marketplace, although BDAG 14-15 s.v. ἀγοραῖος 1 gives the meaning, by extension, as “rabble.” Such a description is certainly appropriate in this context. L&N 15.127 translates the phrase “worthless men from the streets.”
On this term, which is a NT hapax legomenon, see BDAG 745 s.v. ὀχλοποιέω.
BDAG 458 s.v. θορυβέω 1 has “set the city in an uproar, start a riot in the city” for the meaning of ἐθορύβουν (ethoruboun) in this verse.
The attack took place at Jason’s house because this was probably the location of the new house church.
Grk “them”; the referents (Paul and Silas) have been specified in the translation for clarity.
BDAG 223 s.v. δῆμος 2 has “in a Hellenistic city, a convocation of citizens called together for the purpose of transacting official business, popular assembly προάγειν εἰς τὸν δ. Ac 17:5.”

verses.zh: 找不着他们，就把耶孙和几个弟兄拉到地方官那里，喊叫说：「那搅乱天下的也到这里来了，
verses.en: When they did not find them, they dragged[NOTE:1] Jason and some of the brothers before the city officials,[NOTE:2] screaming, “These people who have stirred up trouble[NOTE:3] throughout the world[NOTE:4] have come here too,
notes: See BDAG 977-78 s.v. σύρω on this verb. It was used in everyday speech of dragging in fish by a net, or dragging away someone’s (presumably) dead body (Paul in Acts 14:19).

L&N 37.93 defines πολιτάρχης (politarchēs) as “a public official responsible for administrative matters within a town or city and a member of the ruling council of such a political unit—‘city official’” (see also BDAG 845 s.v.).

Or “rebellion.” BDAG 72 s.v. ἀναστατόω has “disturb, trouble, upset,” but in light of the references in the following verse to political insurrection, “stirred up rebellion” would also be appropriate.

Or “the empire.” This was a way of referring to the Roman empire (BDAG 699 s.v. οἰκουμένη 2.b).sn Throughout the world. Note how some of those present had knowledge of what had happened elsewhere. Word about Paul and his companions and their message was spreading.

verses.zh: 耶孙收留他们。这些人都违背凯撒的命令，说另有一个王耶稣。」
verses.en: and[NOTE:1] Jason has welcomed them as guests! They[NOTE:2] are all acting against Caesar’s[NOTE:3] decrees, saying there is another king named[NOTE:4] Jesus!”[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “whom.” Because of the awkwardness in English of having two relative clauses follow one another (“who have stirred up trouble…whom Jason has welcomed”) the relative pronoun here (“whom”) has been replaced by the conjunction “and,” creating a clause that is grammatically coordinate but logically subordinate in the translation.
Grk “and they.” Because of the length of the Greek sentence, the conjunction καί (kai) has not been translated here. Instead a new English sentence is begun.
Or “the emperor’s” (“Caesar” is a title for the Roman emperor).
The word “named” is not in the Greek text, but is supplied for clarity.
Acting…saying…Jesus. The charges are serious, involving sedition (Luke 23:2). If the political charges were true, Rome would have to react.

verses.zh: 众人和地方官听见这话，就惊慌了；
verses.en: They caused confusion among[NOTE:1] the crowd and the city officials[NOTE:2] who heard these things.
notes: Grk “They troubled the crowd and the city officials,” but this could be understood to mean “they bothered” or “they annoyed.” In reality the Jewish instigators managed to instill doubt and confusion into both the mob and the officials by their false charges of treason. Verse 8 suggests the charges raised again Paul, Silas, Jason, and the others were false.

L&N 37.93 defines πολιτάρχης (politarchēs) as “a public official responsible for administrative matters within a town or city and a member of the ruling council of such a political unit—‘city official.’”

verses.zh: 于是取了耶孙和其余之人的保状，就释放了他们。
verses.en: After[NOTE:1] the city officials[NOTE:2] had received bail[NOTE:3] from Jason and the others, they released them.
notes: Grk “And after.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
Grk “they”; the referent (the city officials) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
That is, “a payment” or “a pledge of security” (BDAG 472 s.v. ἱκανός 1) for which “bail” is the most common contemporary English equivalent.

verses.zh: 弟兄们随即在夜间打发保罗和西拉往庇哩亚去。二人到了，就进入犹太人的会堂。
verses.en: The brothers sent Paul and Silas off to Berea[NOTE:1] at once, during the night. When they arrived,[NOTE:2] they went to the Jewish synagogue.[NOTE:3]
notes: Berea (alternate spelling in NRSV Beroea; Greek Beroia) was a very old city in Macedonia on the river Astraeus about 45 mi (75 km) west of Thessalonica.map For location see JP1-C1; JP2-C1; JP3-C1; JP4-C1.

Grk “who arriving there, went to.” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, the relative pronoun (οἵτινες, hoitines) has been left untranslated and a new English sentence begun. The participle παραγενόμενοι (paragenomenoi) has been taken temporally.
See the note on synagogue in 6:9.

verses.zh: 这地方的人贤于帖撒罗尼迦的人，甘心领受这道，天天考查圣经，要晓得这道是与不是。
verses.en: These Jews[NOTE:1] were more open-minded[NOTE:2] than those in Thessalonica,[NOTE:3] for they eagerly[NOTE:4] received[NOTE:5] the message, examining[NOTE:6] the scriptures carefully every day[NOTE:7] to see if these things were so.
notes: Grk “These”; the referent (the Jews in the synagogue at Berea) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “more willing to learn.” L&N 27.48 and BDAG 404 s.v. εὐγενής 2 both use the term “open-minded” here. The point is that they were more receptive to Paul’s message.
Thessalonica was a city in Macedonia (modern Salonica).map For location see JP1-C1; JP2-C1; JP3-C1; JP4-C1.
Or “willingly,” “readily”; Grk “with all eagerness.”

Grk “who received.” Here the relative pronoun (“who”) has been translated as a pronoun (“they”) preceded by a semicolon, which is less awkward in contemporary English than a relative clause at this point.
This verb (BDAG 66 s.v. ἀνακρίνω 1) refers to careful examination.
BDAG 437 s.v. ἡμέρα 2.c has “every day” for this phrase in this verse.

verses.zh: 所以他们中间多有相信的，又有希腊尊贵的妇女，男子也不少。
verses.en: Therefore many of them believed, along with quite a few[NOTE:1] prominent[NOTE:2] Greek women and men.
notes: Grk “not a few”; this use of negation could be misleading to the modern English reader, however, and so has been translated as “quite a few” (which is the actual meaning of the expression).
Or “respected.”

verses.zh: 但帖撒罗尼迦的犹太人知道保罗又在庇哩亚传　神的道，也就往那里去，耸动搅扰众人。
verses.en: But when the Jews from Thessalonica[NOTE:1] heard that Paul had also proclaimed the word of God[NOTE:2] in Berea, they came there too, inciting[NOTE:3] and disturbing[NOTE:4] the crowds.
notes: Thessalonica was a city in Macedonia (modern Salonica).
Grk “that the word of God had also been proclaimed by Paul.” This passive construction has been converted to an active one in the translation for stylistic reasons.
BDAG 911 s.v. σαλεύω 2 has “incite” for σαλεύοντες (saleuontes) in Acts 17:13.sn Inciting. Ironically, it was the Jews who were disturbing the peace, not the Christians.
Or “stirring up” (BDAG 990-91 s.v. ταράσσω 2). The point is the agitation of the crowds.

verses.zh: 当时弟兄们便打发保罗往海边去，西拉和提摩太仍住在庇哩亚。
verses.en: Then the brothers sent Paul away to the coast[NOTE:1] at once, but Silas and Timothy remained in Berea.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “to the sea.” Here ἕως ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν (heōs epi tēn thalassan) must mean “to the edge of the sea,” that is, “to the coast.” Since there is no mention of Paul taking a ship to Athens, he presumably traveled overland. The journey would have been about 340 mi (550 km).
Grk “remained there”; the referent (Berea) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 送保罗的人带他到了雅典，既领了保罗的命，叫西拉和提摩太速速到他这里来，就回去了。
verses.en: Those who accompanied Paul escorted him as far as Athens,[NOTE:1] and after receiving an order for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they left.[NOTE:2]
notes: For location see JP1-C2; JP2-C2; JP3-C2; JP4-C2.
They left. See 1 Thess 3:1-2, which shows they went from here to Thessalonica.

verses.zh: 保罗在雅典等候他们的时候，看见满城都是偶像，就心里着急；
verses.en: While Paul was waiting for them in Athens,[NOTE:1] his spirit was greatly upset[NOTE:2] because he saw[NOTE:3] the city was full of idols.
notes: For location see JP1-C2; JP2-C2; JP3-C2; JP4-C2.

Grk “greatly upset within him,” but the words “within him” were not included in the translation because they are redundant in English. See L&N 88.189. The term could also be rendered “infuriated.”sn His spirit was greatly upset. See Rom 1:18-32 for Paul’s feelings about idolatry. Yet he addressed both Jews and Gentiles with tact and reserve.
Or “when he saw.” The participle θεωροῦντος (theōrountos) has been translated as a causal adverbial participle; it could also be translated as temporal.

verses.zh: 于是在会堂里与犹太人和虔敬的人，并每日在市上所遇见的人，辩论。
verses.en: So he was addressing[NOTE:1] the Jews and the God-fearing Gentiles[NOTE:2] in the synagogue,[NOTE:3] and in the marketplace[NOTE:4] every day[NOTE:5] those who happened to be there.
notes: Although the word διελέξατο (dielexato; from διαλέγομαι, dialegomai) is frequently translated “reasoned,” “disputed,” or “argued,” this sense comes from its classical meaning where it was used of philosophical disputation, including the Socratic method of questions and answers. However, there does not seem to be contextual evidence for this kind of debate in Acts 17:17. As G. Schrenk (TDNT 2:94-95) points out, “What is at issue is the address which any qualified member of a synagogue might give.” Other examples of this may be found in the NT in Matt 4:23 and Mark 1:21.

Or “and the devout,” but this is practically a technical term for the category called God-fearers, Gentiles who worshiped the God of Israel and in many cases kept the Mosaic law, but did not take the final step of circumcision necessary to become a proselyte to Judaism. See further K. G. Kuhn, TDNT 6:732-34, 743-44, and the note on the phrase “God-fearing Greeks” in 17:4.
See the note on synagogue in Acts 6:9.
See the note on marketplace in Acts 16:19.
BDAG 437 s.v. ἡμέρα 2.c has “every day” for this phrase in this verse.

verses.zh: 还有伊壁鸠鲁和斯多亚两门的学士，与他争论。有的说：「这胡言乱语的要说甚么？」有的说：「他似乎是传说外邦鬼神的。」这话是因保罗传讲耶稣与复活的道。
verses.en: Also some of the Epicurean[NOTE:1] and Stoic[NOTE:2] philosophers were conversing[NOTE:3] with him, and some were asking,[NOTE:4] “What does this foolish babbler[NOTE:5] want to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign gods.”[NOTE:6] (They said this because he was proclaiming the good news about Jesus and the resurrection.)[NOTE:7]
notes: An Epicurean was a follower of the philosophy of Epicurus, who founded a school in Athens about 300 b.c. Although the Epicureans saw the aim of life as pleasure, they were not strictly hedonists because they defined pleasure as the absence of pain. Along with this, they desired the avoidance of trouble and freedom from annoyances. They saw organized religion as evil, especially the belief that the gods punished evildoers in an afterlife. In keeping with this, they were unable to accept Paul’s teaching about the resurrection.

A Stoic was a follower of the philosophy founded by Zeno (342-270 b.c.), a Phoenician who came to Athens and modified the philosophical system of the Cynics he found there. The Stoics rejected the Epicurean ideal of pleasure, stressing virtue instead. The Stoics emphasized responsibility for voluntary actions and believed risks were worth taking, but thought the actual attainment of virtue was difficult. They also believed in providence.
BDAG 956 s.v. συμβάλλω 1 has “converse, confer” here.
Grk “saying.”

Or “ignorant show-off.” The traditional English translation of σπερμολόγος (spermologos) is given in L&N 33.381 as “foolish babbler.” However, an alternate view is presented in L&N 27.19, “(a figurative extension of meaning of a term based on the practice of birds in picking up seeds) one who acquires bits and pieces of relatively extraneous information and proceeds to pass them off with pretense and show—‘ignorant show-off, charlatan.’” A similar view is given in BDAG 937 s.v. σπερμολόγος: “in pejorative imagery of persons whose communication lacks sophistication and seems to pick up scraps of information here and there scrapmonger, scavenger…Engl. synonyms include ‘gossip’, ‘babbler’, chatterer’; but these terms miss the imagery of unsystematic gathering.”

The meaning of this phrase is not clear. Literally it reads “strange deities” (see BDAG 210 s.v. δαιμόνιον 1). The note of not being customary is important. In the ancient world what was new was suspicious. The plural δαιμονίων (daimoniōn, “deities”) shows the audience grappling with Paul’s teaching that God was working through Jesus.
This is a parenthetical note by the author.

gr.gloss: he was proclaiming the gospel of

verses.zh: 他们就把他带到亚略•巴古，说：「你所讲的这新道，我们也可以知道吗？
verses.en: So they took Paul and[NOTE:1] brought him to the Areopagus,[NOTE:2] saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are proclaiming?
notes: Grk “him”; the referent (Paul) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Or “to the council of the Areopagus.” See also the term in v. 22.sn The Areopagus has been traditionally understood as reference to a rocky hill near the Acropolis in Athens, although this place may well have been located in the marketplace at the foot of the hill (L&N 93.412; BDAG 129 s.v. ῎Αρειος πάγος). This term does not refer so much to the place, however, as to the advisory council of Athens known as the Areopagus, which dealt with ethical, cultural, and religious matters, including the supervision of education and controlling the many visiting lecturers. Thus it could be translated the council of the Areopagus. See also the term in v. 22.

verses.zh: 因为你有些奇怪的事传到我们耳中，我们愿意知道这些事是甚么意思。」
verses.en: For you are bringing some surprising things[NOTE:1] to our ears, so we want to know what they[NOTE:2] mean.”
notes: BDAG 684 s.v. ξενίζω 2 translates the substantival participle ξενίζοντα (xenizonta) as “astonishing things Ac 17:20.”
Grk “these things,” but since the referent (“surprising things”) is so close, the repetition of “these things” sounds redundant in English, so the pronoun “they” was substituted in the translation.

verses.zh: （雅典人和住在那里的客人都不顾别的事，只将新闻说说听听。）
verses.en: (All the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there used to spend their time[NOTE:1] in nothing else than telling[NOTE:2] or listening to something new.)[NOTE:3]
notes: The imperfect verb ηὐκαίρουν (ēukairoun) has been translated as a customary or habitual imperfect.
BDAG 406-7 s.v. εὐκαιρέω has “used to spend their time in nothing else than telling Ac 17:21.”
This is a parenthetical note by the author. The reference to newness may be pejorative.

verses.zh: 保罗站在亚略•巴古当中，说：「众位雅典人哪，我看你们凡事很敬畏鬼神。
verses.en: So Paul stood[NOTE:1] before the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I see that you are very religious[NOTE:2] in all respects.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “standing…said.” The participle ζηλώσαντες (zēlōsantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

The term δεισιδαιμονεστέρους (deisidaimonesterous) is difficult. On the one hand it can have the positive sense of “devout,” but on the other hand it can have the negative sense of “superstitious” (BDAG 216 s.v. δεισιδαίμων). As part of a laudatory introduction (the technical rhetorical term for this introduction was capatatio), the term is probably positive here. It may well be a “backhanded” compliment, playing on the ambiguity.
BDAG 513 s.v. κατά B.6 translates the phrase κατὰ πάντα (kata panta) as “in all respects.”

verses.zh: 我游行的时候，观看你们所敬拜的，遇见一座坛，上面写着『未识之神』。你们所不认识而敬拜的，我现在告诉你们。
verses.en: For as I went around and observed closely your objects of worship,[NOTE:1] I even found an altar with this inscription:[NOTE:2] ‘To an unknown god.’ Therefore what you worship without knowing it,[NOTE:3] this I proclaim to you.
notes: Or “your sanctuaries.” L&N 53.54 gives “sanctuary” (place of worship) as an alternate meaning for the word σεβάσματα (sebasmata).

Grk “on which was written,” but since it would have been carved in stone, it is more common to speak of an “inscription” in English. To simplify the English the relative construction with a passive verb (“on which was inscribed”) was translated as a prepositional phrase with a substantive (“inscription”).

BDAG 13 s.v. ἀγνοέω 1.b has “Abs. ὅ ἀγνοοῦντες εὐσεβεῖτε what you worship without knowing it (on the subject matter Maximus Tyr. 11, 5e: all sorts of philosophers ἴσασιν οὐκ ἑκόντες καὶ λέγουσιν ἄκοντες sc. τὸ θεῖον = they know and name God without intending to do so) Ac 17:23.” Paul, in typical Jewish Christian style, informs them of the true God, of whom their idols are an ignorant reflection.

verses.zh: 创造宇宙和其中万物的　神，既是天地的主，就不住人手所造的殿，
verses.en: The God who made the world and everything in it,[NOTE:1] who is[NOTE:2] Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by human hands,[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “all the things that are in it.” The speech starts with God as Creator, like 14:15.

Or “because he is.” The participle ὑπάρχων (huparchōn) could be either adjectival, modifying οὗτος (houtos, “who is Lord…”) or adverbial of cause (“because he is Lord…”). Since the participle διδούς (didous) in v. 25 appears to be clearly causal in force, it is preferable to understand ὑπάρχων as adjectival in this context.

On the statement does not live in temples made by human hands compare Acts 7:48. This has implications for idols as well. God cannot be represented by them or, as the following clause also suggests, served by human hands.

verses.zh: 也不用人手服事，好像缺少甚么；自己倒将生命、气息、万物，赐给万人。
verses.en: nor is he served by human hands, as if he needed anything,[NOTE:1] because he himself gives life and breath and everything to everyone.[NOTE:2]
notes: L&N 57.45 has “nor does he need anything more that people can supply by working for him.”
Grk “he himself gives to all [people] life and breath and all things.”

verses.zh: 他从一本（本：有古卷是血脉）造出万族的人，住在全地上，并且预先定准他们的年限和所住的疆界，
verses.en: From one man[NOTE:1] he made every nation of the human race[NOTE:2] to inhabit the entire earth,[NOTE:3] determining their set times[NOTE:4] and the fixed limits of the places where they would live,[NOTE:5]
notes: The one man refers to Adam (the word “man” is understood).
Or “mankind.” BDAG 276 s.v. ἔθνος 1 has “every nation of humankind Ac 17:26.”
Grk “to live over all the face of the earth.”

BDAG 884-85 s.v. προστάσσω has “(οἱ) προστεταγμένοι καιροί (the) fixed times Ac 17:26” here, but since the following phrase is also translated “fixed limits,” this would seem redundant in English, so the word “set” has been used instead.
Grk “the boundaries of their habitation.” L&N 80.5 has “fixed limits of the places where they would live” for this phrase.

verses.zh: 要叫他们寻求　神，或者可以揣摩而得，其实他离我们各人不远；
verses.en: so that they would search for God and perhaps grope around[NOTE:1] for him and find him,[NOTE:2] though he is[NOTE:3] not far from each one of us.
notes: See BDAG 1097-98 s.v. ψηλαφάω, which lists “touch, handle” and “to feel around for, grope for” as possible meanings.
Perhaps grope around for him and find him. The pagans’ struggle to know God is the point here. Conscience alone is not good enough.
The participle ὑπάρχοντα (huparchonta) has been translated as a concessive adverbial participle.

verses.zh: 我们生活、动作、存留，都在乎他。就如你们作诗的，有人说：『我们也是他所生的。』
verses.en: For in him we live and move about[NOTE:1] and exist, as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we too are his offspring.’[NOTE:2]
notes: According to L&N 15.1, “A strictly literal translation of κινέω in Ac 17:28 might imply merely moving from one place to another. The meaning, however, is generalized movement and activity; therefore, it may be possible to translate κινούμεθα as ‘we come and go’ or ‘we move about’ or even ‘we do what we do.’”
This quotation is from Aratus (ca. 310-245 b.c.), Phaenomena 5. Paul asserted a general relationship and accountability to God for all humanity.

verses.zh: 我们既是　神所生的，就不当以为　神的神性像人用手艺、心思所雕刻的金、银、石。
verses.en: So since we are God’s offspring, we should not think the deity[NOTE:1] is like gold or silver or stone, an image[NOTE:2] made by human[NOTE:3] skill[NOTE:4] and imagination.[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “the divine being.” BDAG 446 s.v. θεῖος 1.b has “divine being, divinity” here.
Or “a likeness.” Again idolatry is directly attacked as an affront to God and a devaluation of him.
Grk “by the skill and imagination of man,” but ἀνθρώπου (anthrōpou) has been translated as an attributive genitive.
Or “craftsmanship” (cf. BDAG 1001 s.v. τέχνη).
Or “thought.” BDAG 336 s.v. ἐνθύμησις has “thought, reflection, idea” as the category of meaning here, but in terms of creativity (as in the context) the imaginative faculty is in view.

verses.zh: 世人蒙昧无知的时候，　神并不监察，如今却吩咐各处的人都要悔改。
verses.en: Therefore, although God has overlooked[NOTE:1] such times of ignorance,[NOTE:2] he now commands all people[NOTE:3] everywhere to repent,[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “has deliberately paid no attention to.”
Or “times when people did not know.”
Here ἀνθρώποις (anthrōpois) has been translated as a generic noun (“people”).
He now commands all people everywhere to repent. God was now asking all mankind to turn to him. No nation or race was excluded.

verses.zh: 因为他已经定了日子，要藉着他所设立的人按公义审判天下，并且叫他从死里复活，给万人作可信的凭据。」
verses.en: because he has set[NOTE:1] a day on which he is going to judge the world[NOTE:2] in righteousness, by a man whom he designated,[NOTE:3] having provided proof to everyone by raising[NOTE:4] him from the dead.”
notes: Or “fixed.”
The world refers to the whole inhabited earth.

Or “appointed.” BDAG 723 s.v. ὁρίζω 2.b has “of persons appoint, designate, declare: God judges the world ἐν ἀνδρὶ ᾧ ὥρισεν through a man whom he has appointed Ac 17:31.”sn A man whom he designated. Jesus is put in the position of eschatological judge. As judge of the living and the dead, he possesses divine authority (Acts 10:42).
The participle ἀναστήσας (anastēsas) indicates means here.

verses.zh: 众人听见从死里复活的话，就有讥诮他的；又有人说：「我们再听你讲这个吧！」
verses.en: Now when they heard about[NOTE:1] the resurrection from the dead, some began to scoff,[NOTE:2] but others said, “We will hear you again about this.”
notes: The participle ἀκούσαντες (akousantes) has been taken temporally.
L&N 33.408 has “some scoffed (at him) Ac 17:32” for ἐχλεύαζον (echleuazon) here; the imperfect verb has been translated as an ingressive imperfect (“began to scoff”).

verses.zh: 于是保罗从他们当中出去了。
verses.en: So Paul left the Areopagus.[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “left out of their midst”; the referent (the Areopagus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 但有几个人贴近他，信了主，其中有亚略•巴古的官丢尼修，并一个妇人，名叫大马哩，还有别人一同信从。
verses.en: But some people[NOTE:1] joined him[NOTE:2] and believed. Among them[NOTE:3] were Dionysius, who was a member of the Areopagus,[NOTE:4] a woman[NOTE:5] named Damaris, and others with them.
notes: Although the Greek word here is ἀνήρ (anēr), which normally refers to males, husbands, etc., in this particular context it must have a generic force similar to that of ἄνθρωπος (anthrōpos), since “a woman named Damaris” is mentioned specifically as being part of this group (cf. BDAG 79 s.v. ἀνήρ 1.a).

Grk “joining him, believed.” The participle κολληθέντες (kollēthentes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. On the use of this verb in Acts, see 5:13; 8:29; 9:26; 10:28.
Grk “among whom.” Due to the length of the Greek sentence, the relative pronoun (“whom”) has been translated as a third person plural pronoun (“them”) and a new sentence begun in the translation.

Grk “the Areopagite” (a member of the council of the Areopagus). The noun “Areopagite” is not in common usage today in English. It is clearer to use a descriptive phrase “a member of the Areopagus” (L&N 11.82). However, this phrase alone can be misleading in English: “Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus, and a woman named Damaris” could be understood to refer to three people (Dionysius, an unnamed member of the Areopagus, and Damaris) rather than only two. Converting the descriptive phrase to a relative clause in English (“who was a member of the Areopagus”) removes the ambiguity.
Grk “and a woman,” but this καί (kai) has not been translated since English normally uses a coordinating conjunction only between the last two elements in a series of three or more.
